en: Preface to the *Yigao of the Land of Bliss*, compiled by the Śramaṇa Zongxiao of Shizhi in Siming. Preface to the *Yigao of the Land of Bliss*:
I have resolutely set my will upon the practice of the Pure Land, vowing that all sentient beings shall be equally encompassed so that they may together return to the realm of reality. Therefore...
I have compiled this *Collection of Texts on the Land of Bliss* (*Lebang wenlei*),
circulating it beyond the secular world; it includes fragments of texts and single points of meaning,
as well as whatever I have seen or heard that may be beneficial for supporting those who cultivate the Pure Land.
Furthermore, it was subsequently recorded as the *Yibao* (Supplementary Drafts) of the Land of Bliss;
this was modeled after the Confucian tradition of collecting lost texts (*Shiyi*).
Some of its phrasing is quite prolix.
Thus, I have briefly set forth the essential outlines;
although it is not yet complete,
I hope that others may gain some insight from it.
On the morning of the first day of spring in the year of Jiǎzǐ,
I took up my brush and wrote this preface. Zōngxiǎo has compiled the two books on the Land of Bliss (Lèbāng),
arranging them according to their subject matter and exhausting the topics with their respective titles.
Reflecting on this in tranquility:
this book is specifically intended to guide all sentient beings toward the Pure Land;
it may also be titled "A Record of Aspiration for the Land of Bliss."
Indeed, every person inherently possesses the Land of Bliss within their own mind.
Why rely on arduous toil or the painful practice of cultivation and realization?
Alas! To enter the various realms of existence in vain!
After a long time, one forgets the origin;
this was a lament of those of old.
Behold the decayed bones buried by the roadside.
Among these, many are those who have not yet returned [to the Way];
this is precisely what is meant here. Fortunately, the Buddhas and Patriarchs have opened up and crossed the essential ford, so that we may now gather and extract [these teachings].
By assisting and encouraging others to give rise to faith,
one causes those who leap forward in their practice to clearly understand the path home.
To have no hesitation between the two diverging paths of birth-and-death is the essential Way;
it is also called "The Return to the Will."
It is truly found herein.
If the reader indeed does not fail their hometown upon returning,
they will finally believe that the lotus-like superior friends have been waiting for a long time.
Gather your body and mind and return home well.
Exert yourselves! Exert yourselves!
King Śuddhodana and seventy thousand members of the Śākya clan were all reborn in the Pure Land. (From the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, Fascicle 76).
The Buddha addressed his father, King Śuddhodana, saying:
"Within the Buddha-dharma,
you should practice with diligent vigor and cultivate heedfulness."
"Great King,
all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma. The King said,
"If all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma, then..."
"All sentient beings should also be Buddhas.
The Buddha said,
"If one does not regard sentient beings with negligence or inverted views, [they are indeed Buddhas]."
This, Great King, is the Buddha.
All phenomena are without birth, without movement, and without fluctuation.
There is nothing to be grasped and nothing to be relinquished;
there are no characteristics and no intrinsic nature.
"Great King,
you should now settle your mind within this Dharma;
do not place your trust in others."
When the Buddha preached this Dharma,
the king and seventy thousand Śākyas attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested a smile.
The bhikṣu Aśvajit questioned the Buddha with a verse.
The Buddha replied:
"I manifest this smile of quiescence."
Aśvajit, listen attentively;
I shall now speak according to reality.
This is the definitive wisdom of the Śākya clan.
All phenomena are ungraspable;
the Śākyas have all realized this.
Therefore, regarding the Buddha-dharma, [they are liberated].
With their minds firmly settled in certainty, after passing away from among human beings,
they shall be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss,
where they will personally attend upon Amitāyus.
Attaining Bodhi through Fearlessness.
The Honored Title of the Tathāgata Twelve Radiances. The Great Original Sūtra of Immeasurable Life.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
The radiance of Amitāyus Buddha is most honored and supreme;
it cannot be equaled by the radiance of any other buddha.
It may illuminate as many as a hundred buddha-worlds.
It may illuminate a thousand buddha-worlds;
to speak of it in brief,
it illuminates as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
Therefore, the Buddha of Immeasurable Life is also called the Buddha of Immeasurable Light,
the Buddha of Boundless Light,
and the Buddha of Unobstructed Light.
The Buddha Apratigha-prabha,
the Buddha Jvalendra-prabha,
and the Buddha Viśuddha-prabha.
The Buddha Joyful Light,
the Buddha Wisdom Light,
and the Buddha Uninterrupted Light.
The Buddha Inconceivable Light,
the Buddha Incomparable Light,
and the Buddha Surpassing the Sun and Moon Light.
Any sentient beings who encounter this light will have their three impurities eliminated,
and their bodies and minds will become supple and pliant.
In the Land of Amitābha Buddha, the Dharma of the Three Vehicles is taught. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The Buddha appears in this world of the five turbidities and divides the path of the One Vehicle into three vehicles."
If that is so, Amitābha Buddha was not born into this world of the five turbidities; why, then,
did he still establish the three vehicles?
Answer: When the Buddhas first resolve their minds [on enlightenment],
they see all Buddhas delivering sentient beings by means of the three vehicles.
He made this vow himself, saying:
"I, too, shall now deliver sentient beings by means of the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.
Furthermore, the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith) states that in the Pure Land, the water birds and the trees and forests preach the Dharma.
As for the sound produced by the trees made of the seven treasures when stirred by the wind in the Pure Land, it is intended to make the Dharma easy for sentient beings to hear.
Question: [Why is this so?]
The Buddhas possess immeasurable supernormal powers;
why do they not transform [themselves] into [other forms]?
Why is it necessary for the sound to come from the trees?
Answer: Sentient beings are exceedingly numerous.
If the Buddha were to manifest his body in every place, [he would be unable to save them all].
Sentient beings do not believe;
they regard it as a magical illusion,
and their minds lack reverence.
There are sentient beings who,
upon hearing the Dharma from humans, do not awaken to it;
yet if they hear the Dharma from animals, they believe and accept it.
Because they are rare;
furthermore, because the minds of animals are straightforward and not deceitful. Some say:
Animals are sentient beings; they all possess the capacity for deception.
Since trees lack consciousness yet produce sounds, [how much more so do animals].
Thus, all believed and accepted the ninety-three fascicles of the treatise.

Regarding the monk who asked the lecturer on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*: the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) mentions a monk who questioned the lecturer on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
He asked the presiding lecturer of the *Amitābha Sūtra*:
"It is said that the waterfowl and the trees all constantly recollect the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. How is this so?"
The lecturer said:
"Master Ji’s Way holds that a true friend does not wait to be invited."
It was like a mother rushing to her infant.
The monk asked,
"What is it that constitutes a true friend who does not wait to be invited?"
Fayan spoke on their behalf, saying:
"These are the words of Master Ji.
This is the *Verses for Praising the Buddha* from the *Great Text of the Maitreya Repentance Ritual*. The *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra*, composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna."
The fourth fascicle lists the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions to whom one pays homage during the Lotus Repentance,
each accompanied by verses of praise.
The verses for praising the Buddha in the *Da-ben Mituo chan* (Great Text Amitābha Repentance) are derived from that very source.
Ciyun then selected and revised the text,
composing it to praise Amitābha on the principle that the Way of all Buddhas is one and the same.
The verse says:
"His physical marks are like a mountain of gold.
This praises the Buddha Kuśalamati of the eastern quarter.
"His face is like the pure full moon.
This is the verse praising the Buddha Candanagandha of the southern quarter.
"The radiance of his body and the brilliance of his wisdom."
His illumination is boundless;
he crushes the hosts of Māra’s enemies and skillfully transforms all humans and devas.
These four lines praise the Buddha Amitābha of the Western Quarter:
"By boarding the vessel of the Eightfold Path,
he is able to cross the sea that is so difficult to traverse."
"By hearing his name one attains non-retrogression;
for this reason, I prostrate in homage.
These four lines praise the Buddha Lakṣaṇaguṇasāgara of the northern direction.
The treatise is contained in the Zi-case.

[It concerns] the Verses for Praising the Buddha from the Shorter Amitābha Repentance Ritual. The Verses for Praising the Buddha from the Shorter Amitābha Repentance Ritual state, according to the Śrīmālā-sūtra:
In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was King Prasenajit; [the daughter] of Queen Mallikā...
Her name was Śrīmālā;
she was the wife of the King of Ayodhyā. Mālikā said:
"My daughter is intelligent and of sharp faculties;
if she were to see the Buddha,
she would surely understand the Dharma quickly."
He immediately dispatched a messenger with a letter.
Upon receiving the letter,
Śrīmālā spoke this verse:
I look up with reverence to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who has appeared for the sake of the entire world;
may he likewise extend his compassionate pity and surely grant that I may behold him.
As soon as this verse was spoken—
Śākyamuni then appeared in the air.
Vaśiṣṭhā further praised him, saying:
"The Tathāgata’s wondrous form-body..."
In the world there is none equal to you;
you are peerless and inconceivable.
Therefore, I now pay homage to you.
The form of the Tathāgata is inexhaustible,
and his wisdom is likewise so;
all phenomena are eternally abiding.
Therefore, I take refuge.
Śrīmālā spoke these verses to express her innermost intent,
and the Buddha immediately bestowed upon her a specific prophecy.
The title "Universally Radiant Tathāgata" and so forth refers to this verse used for praising the Buddha in the *Fourfold Holy Repentance* (Sisheng Chan) in its shorter Indian version.
The portion from "By the power of great wisdom and great vows" onwards was composed by the Master of Repentance.
King Prasenajit Contemplates the True Reality of the Buddha. In the *Renyang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra), the Buddha asked King Prasenajit:
"By what marks do you contemplate the Tathāgata?"
The King said,
"Contemplate the true mark of the body;
contemplate the Buddha in the same way."
There is no prior limit,
no subsequent limit,
and no middle limit.
It does not abide in the three periods of time,
nor is it separate from the three periods of time;
it does not abide in the five aggregates.
Not separate from the five aggregates,
not abiding in the four great elements,
and not separate from the four great elements.
They do not abide in the six sense bases,
nor are they separated from the six sense bases;
they do not abide in the three realms.
It is not apart from the three realms,
yet it is beyond seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing;
it is where the sphere of mental activity ceases.
The path of language is cut off;
it is identical with the limit of reality and equal to the nature of phenomena.
"I contemplate the body of the Tathāgata by means of these marks.
The Buddha said,
"It should be contemplated in this way."
If one contemplates otherwise, it is called wrong contemplation.
Regarding the Five Expedient Gates of Mindfulness of the Buddha by the Great Master Zhiyi: the Tiantai Great Master Zhiyi showed people the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha.
There are five skillful means;
those who contemplate the West and seek rebirth therein must certainly cultivate them.
Therefore, the text says:
"In general, dwelling the mind on a single object is called 'concentrated-mind dhyāna' (niṣpanda-dhyāna)."
This means that when the practitioner recollects the Buddha,
they clearly contemplate the Tathāgata’s jade-like brow-hair and golden marks,
which are immovable and tranquil, perfectly luminous and penetratingly clear.
Furthermore, although one previously concentrated the mind,
because the practice was not yet habitual, it was not noticed when it wandered away; now,
one must restrain it and cause it to return to the object of attention— the golden image.
This is called the dhyāna of restraining the mind.
Furthermore, attaining concentration by restraining the mind is not contemplation according to principle.
All these belong to the cultivation of phenomena.
Now, if we examine their essence:
fundamentally empty, who can congeal them, and who can restrain them?
The absence of both Buddha and thought is called "contemplation of the true essence" (*tizenzen*). Furthermore,
although the preceding stage was the contemplation of the true essence, [it is not yet complete].
One still remains stagnant in empty quiescence;
the immeasurable names and characteristics remain obscure and unknown.
Now, one takes non-attainment as the skillful means.
Entering the provisional from emptiness,
one penetrates all phenomena; thus,
one is not deluded or disturbed by the defilements of emptiness.
This is called the dhyāna of skillful means (*upāya*).
Furthermore, although the preceding [stages] involved realizing the reality of the essence as well as following conditions through skillful means,
each remained based on either emptiness or existence, thus not departing from the two extremes.
Now, when one observes with clarity that the root of contention and turmoil is fundamentally without characteristics,
the path of names and words is severed,
and even thought is cut off.
This is called the dhyāna that ceases the discrimination of the two extremes.
These five gates proceed from the shallow to the deep;
however, the essential nature of Perfect Enlightenment is fundamentally devoid of such gradations.
Yet their degrees of depth and shallowness remain distinct.

In the *Nianfo Chanmen* (The Dhyāna Gate of Buddha-Recollection) of the Four Teachings, Master Zhiyi teaches the departure from thought. Although, as mentioned above, one employs the five gates of skillful means to contemplate the true body of the Buddha, [the ultimate goal is the cessation of conceptualization].
Furthermore, one must clarify the detachment from conceptual thought within the four teachings in order to demonstrate the intent of rejecting the partial and embracing the perfect.
Thus, the text says:
Now, the mind does not arise in isolation;
it must necessarily depend upon conditions for its arising.
When a practitioner recollects the Buddha, [the mind arises in this manner].
The mental faculty serves as the cause;
the light from the Tathāgata’s ūrṇā-kośa serves as the condition.
The thought thus aroused is the dharma that is produced.
To contemplate these three marks as shifting and changing, not abiding for even a single thought-moment,
and to analyze them until they are seen as empty—
this is the mindfulness of the Buddha according to the Hīnayāna of the Tripiṭaka Teaching.
Immediately upon contemplating the Buddha, the mind arises;
yet both that which gives rise [to it] and that which is given rise to are entirely empty.
It is only through delusion that one says "the mind arises."
Upon realizing its nature, it is emptiness itself;
the observed form of the Buddha is like a reflection in a mirror—
neither Buddha nor thought.
This is precisely the Mahayana practice of mindfulness of the Buddha according to the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao). It is the arising of the mind of contemplative mindfulness of the Buddha;
it is a provisional designation (prajñapti).
The mind of provisional names clearly mirrors immeasurable names and characteristics;
one thoroughly understands that this mind possesses the Tathāgatagarbha.
Throughout kalpas, one cuts off and realizes;
departing from extremes, one reveals the Middle Way;
there is no Buddha and no thought.
This is precisely the nianfo (recollection of the Buddha) of the Distinct Teaching of the Mahayana.
It is the contemplation that when the mind of nianfo arises,
it is simultaneously empty, simultaneously provisional, and simultaneously the Middle Way.

Whether it be the sense faculties or the sensory objects, all are the dharma-realm; the Buddhas of all lands and dust-motes illuminate them in a single thought-moment, and they universally respond to sentient beings of the six realms in a single kṣaṇa.
This is the very first mind.
Now one begins to realize this awakening:
it is like a person of great merit who takes a stone and transforms it into a jewel;
the mind has no thought of discarding it to seek elsewhere for that which is free from thought.
This is precisely the middle within the extremes;
there is neither Buddha nor thought.
This is the mindfulness of the Buddha according to the Perfect Teaching of the Mahāyāna.
The *Ratnavyūha Sūtra* clarifies that the Tathāgata is realized through sudden awakening;
this is precisely what is meant here.
Regarding the visualization of Amitābha’s sixteen-foot body and thirty-two marks, the eighth section on the "Contemplation of the Image" in the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* states:
Therefore, when a practitioner brings the Buddha to mind, this very mind is itself the thirty-two primary marks and eighty secondary signs.
As it says: "When one wishes to visualize that Buddha, one should first form a mental image."
Regarding the passage on "seeing a precious image with eyes closed or open" and so forth, the ninth chapter of the *Contemplation Sūtra*, "The Contemplation of the True Dharmakāya," states:

"Contemplate the eighty-four thousand marks and signs of Amitābha. It further says: "Contemplate the eighty-four thousand marks and signs of Amitābha. (The *Contemplation Sūtra*, Chapter Nine, "The Contemplation of the True Dharmakāya") states: [as above].
The body of Amitāyus Buddha is like the color of the Jambūnada gold of the Yāma Heaven, numbering hundreds of thousands of millions of billions;
the height of the Buddha’s body is sixty million billion nayuta *gaṅgā*-sands of *yojanas*.
Regarding the statement that Amitāyus Buddha possesses eighty-four thousand marks,
and that each mark has eighty-four thousand secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*),
the *Sijiao miaozong* (The Wondrous Commentary on the Four Clarifications) explains as follows:
In the previous eighth contemplation, one contemplates the image;
it then resembles the Buddha’s body.
Now, because one faces that resemblance, it is called "real."
However, this physical form is the true Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya);
it should be understood as the "Lordly" (jushi) body, and is also called the "Distinguished and Exalted" (zunte).
It is also called the "Victorious Response" (saṃbhogakāya).
Yet it is termed the "Dharmakāya" because both the retributive and responsive [bodies] are entirely inherent within the nature.
The subsequent text further states:
"The eighty thousand marks and signs of Amitābha are the wondrous and extraordinary body manifested by that Tathāgata."
The deep-stage *nien-fo samādhi* (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) increases;
it is not within the reach of the mental power of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
It further states:
The practitioner should know that the three contemplations cultivated from the "contemplation of the sun" onwards are shared with the dhyāna of phenomena (vastu-dhyāna).
Subduing the thoughts of the triple world,
one uses wondrous contemplation to break through the thoughts regarding forms; thus,
one immediately ascends to the seventh stage, the stage of faith.
Having attained this stage,
one is then able to contemplate the Buddha’s true Dharma-body,
wherein the eighty thousand marks manifest.
This is what is called the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha.
The marks manifested through such a perfect contemplation are truly extraordinary.
This is truly not the appearance commonly seen by ordinary beings or those of the Lesser Vehicle who view it as a physical body.
Regarding the sixteen-foot image atop Amitābha’s pond, the thirteenth chapter of the *Contemplation Sūtra*, "The Contemplation of Various Features," states:
If one wishes to give rise to a sincere mind for rebirth in the Western Land,
one should first visualize the image of the Buddha, one zhang and six chi in height, upon the surface of the water.
As previously described, the physical dimensions of Amitāyus Buddha are boundless.
This is not within the reach of the mental power of ordinary beings, as previously stated;
it is as described in the "Contemplation of the Eighth Image," namely,
the contemplation of Amitābha’s thirty-two primary marks and eighty secondary signs.
The *Miaozongji* (Exegesis on the Sublime Commentary) states:
"Regarding the contemplation of the Buddha’s body through various mental images (*jixiangguan*), there are briefly two intentions.
First, for those who have not succeeded in the previous contemplation of the eighty thousand marks and signs."
He then instructs them to set aside the vast [cosmic body] and contemplate the sixteen-foot [form].
Second, having contemplated the person who has already perfected the eighty thousand excellent marks,
he further instructs them to contemplate the superior and inferior transformative functions pervading the worlds of the ten directions.
This causes one's spiritual rank to advance.
Through the cultivation of the six perfections and myriad practices,
the Buddhas realize as their fruit the originally inherent three bodies in essence.
Now, Amitābha as the sixteen-foot *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is the response body;
[Amitābha] as six million *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sands of *yojana*s is the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body);
that which is neither retribution nor response is the *dharmakāya*.
The Dharma-body pervades all places. Now,
while Amitābha’s reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is thus vast and sublime,
the mental conceptions of ordinary beings below are weak and inferior.
One must not view this superficially. In the Buddha’s era,
people possessed sharp faculties like those of Vaidehī,
who received the Buddha’s instruction on the sixteen contemplations of the realms.
Following these words, one advances in practice until reaching the eighth stage of the semblance contemplation (*pratibimba-bhāvanā*);
it is only upon entering the seventh level of faith (*śraddhā*) that one attains universal contemplation.
Moreover, in this final age, those of dull faculties cannot immediately contemplate the sublime marks;
they must first contemplate the sixteen-foot form.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"If one wishes to give rise to a sincere mind and reach the Western Land,
one should first visualize the image one zhang and six chi tall above the pond."
The physical dimensions of Amitāyus Buddha are boundless;
they are beyond the reach of the mental power of ordinary beings.
This is the extraordinary and wondrous skillful means of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
The instructions direct one to contemplate the great from the small from a young age;
hence there is this saying. Or it may not be so.
If one were to practice based on the Buddha’s *saṃbhogakāya*,
one would still fail to avoid the peril of gazing at a precipice from afar.
Nowadays, many among both the clergy and the laity do not understand this meaning.
In all rites of praise and visualization, there are none that do not first mention the eighty-four thousand marks and signs;
judging this by the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs,
is this not to overstep the proper order and miss the essential meaning?
A fool such as I certainly dares not venture a conjecture;
fortunately, the holy teachings are fully preserved,
whereby I am able to conduct an examination and comparison.
From this point forward,
one should not reject the words because of the person; rather,
please propagate them in accordance with the teachings and principles.

If one contemplates a single Buddha, all Buddhas will manifest of themselves; if one contemplates a single Buddha, all Buddhas will manifest of themselves. The *Ratnagotravibhāga* (Jewel King Treatise), citing the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, states:
"One becomes deluded due to spatial orientation."
The direction is truly non-turning.
Such being the case,
those who awaken awaken to a single direction.
The various directions are naturally rectified.
One who maintains mindfulness focuses on a single Buddha,
and all Buddhas appear before them.
This refers to the fact that the water does not rise upward,
the moon does not descend downward,
and there is the causal condition of luminous purity.
The bright moon in the void appears in clear water;
that Buddha does not come,
and my body does not go.
Regarding the causal conditions for mindfulness of the Buddha:
the Tathāgata’s precious moon appears within the water of the mind.
Thus, the verse says:
The Bodhisattva is like the cool moon,
wandering through ultimate emptiness;
when the water of sentient beings' minds is pure, [the reflection appears].

Within the manifestation of the shadow of Bodhi, those who recite the name of the Buddha will surely achieve samādhi; those who recite the name of the Buddha will surely achieve [it]. The *Ratnarāśi-śāstra* says:
"One who bathes in the great ocean..."
Just as water used in a hundred rivers [is ultimately one],
those who recite the name of the Buddha will certainly achieve samādhi.
It is just as when a pure pearl is cast into turbid water;
the turbid water cannot fail to become clear.
So too, when the visualization of the Buddha is projected into a distracted mind.
A distracted mind cannot attain Buddhahood;
once one has realized this accord,
both mind and Buddha vanish together.
When both mind and Buddha have perished, then all conditions and all objects are nothing other than samādhi.
Preface to Master Wen’s *Dharmaparyāya on Pure Conduct*. Now, to realize that within the mindless there is mind—this is the gateway to liberation.
Consciousness possesses the non-thought within thought;
abiding neither in being nor non-being,
how could subject and object exist?
This is the state where every thought-moment is perfectly luminous and every mind is empty and tranquil;
were one to remain ignorant of this principle, [one would fail].
Thus, phenomena are perfected within phenomena;
precisely accords with the fundamental principle,
and thereby each gate penetrates the wondrous.
Now, without deviating from ultimate reality, one may demonstrate perfect cultivation,
so that those burdened with heavy loads and traveling far distances may find relief for their shoulders,
and those wandering in confusion at the ford may swiftly ascend to the other shore.
There has never been a method for the contemplation of mindfulness of the Buddha through pure karma that preceded that of the West.
Thus, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
"Although one knows that all Buddha-lands and sentient beings are empty..."
And yet they constantly cultivate the Pure Land and transform sentient beings—
is this not what is meant by that?
I have now, for the sake of laymen and laywomen,
extensively gathered the essential outlines of the sūtras and śāstras to compose this "Dharma Gate of Pure Conduct in the Western Land."
This reveals what they have cultivated,
enabling them to attain its essential course.
Should anyone behold this text, [they shall understand].
Furthermore, those who are unable to give rise to faith and establish practice are like those suffering from a feverish delirium who throw themselves into a latrine;
they merely expose a single strand of hair, seeking to be rescued.
What can be done about this?
Regarding the Dharma-gate of Pure Conduct for those who resolve to attain Bodhicitta and seek rebirth in the Pure Land, it is said:
For all practitioners of the Pure Land path, [the following applies].
One must properly resolve the mind.
If one generates aversion toward the five turbidities for one's own sake while longing for the nine grades [of rebirth],
this contravenes the bodhicitta.
This is the practice of the śrāvakas;
one should not give rise to it.
However, if one gives rise to the mind of great compassion for the sake of sentient beings, [it is appropriate].
I seek to go to that land,
hoping to swiftly achieve the power of the Way and traverse the ten directions with supernormal powers.
To rescue and deliver all beings,
causing them to together realize the Buddha-way,
is to accord with the bodhicitta.
This is the practice of a bodhisattva;
one should resolve to undertake it.
Regarding the mindfulness of the Buddha, it is like a private subject encountering an enlightened sovereign. The Dharma-gate of Pure Conduct says:
Repentance is like diligently polishing an ancient mirror,
gradually clearing away the accumulated dust of successive generations;
mindfulness of the Buddha is like a private audience with an enlightened sovereign.
One suddenly attains the sign of future liberation within the cycle of spring, summer, autumn, and winter,
and amidst the activities of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.
Diligently contemplate the adornments of the Pure Land and constantly keep Amitābha Buddha in mind;
in this way, the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha will manifest before you.
Yang Wuweī’s Preface to the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha-saṃghāṭī-dharma*: The Dharma Master Zhào of the Fohuì Bǎogé Monastery in Qiántáng, for the sake of the five groups of monastics.
He practiced the ritual of repentance for the Pure Land.
Wúwéi zǐ saw it and inscribed the following at its conclusion:
The Pure Land is serene and immaculate;
it cannot be born into through the power of mere vows.
In this turbid world, transgressions and evils abound.
Nothing but repentance can remove it.
A sin is like a tile or a stone;
once cast into water, it will surely sink.

To seek the Buddha by discerning forms and sounds is called a heterodox path. (To seek the Buddha by discerning forms and sounds is called a heterodox path. *Guānjīng yìshū* (Commentary on the Meaning of the *Avalokana Sūtra*) asks:
The Sūtra says:
"If one sees me by means of form,
or seeks me by means of sound."
Such people walk upon a deviant path;
they cannot see the Tathāgata.
Now, when one contemplates the Buddha and recollects the Buddha, is this not seeing through form and seeking through sound?
The answer is:
His thirty-two marks are like the bright moon descending upon a hundred rivers;
his fourfold eloquence and eightfold tones are like a pure resonance emerging from a deep valley.
However, there are those who wade through deep pools to grasp at the moon or enter valleys to seek out echoes;
failing to realize that nature is empty,
they do not see the Buddha.
The realized one is not like this;
having understood that form is no-form,
what prevents him from directing his contemplation toward the countenance of the Sage?
Having realized that sound is non-sound,
how could one be hindered from hearing the wondrous Dharma by the side?
Thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
Physical form is not the Buddha;
sound is likewise so. Yet, it is also not apart from form and sound.
Having witnessed the Buddha’s supernatural powers and beheld these wondrous words,
how could one possibly give rise to the obstruction of doubt?
There are ten types of people in the world who, at the time of death, are unable to recite the Buddha’s name. The *Qunyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts) states:
"In my observation of the world..."
There are ten kinds of people who,
at the end of their lives, will not be able to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
The first is those for whom they do not necessarily encounter virtuous friends.
There is no principle by which they could be exhorted or reminded [to practice].
Second, their bodies are entangled in the suffering of karma,
leaving them no leisure to mindfully recollect the Buddha.

Third, some lose the power of speech due to a localized wind disorder and are unable to recite the name of the Buddha; fourth, those who are deranged and have lost their minds find it difficult to focus their thoughts.
Fifth, encountering water or fire,
one has no leisure for sincere devotion;
sixth, encountering jackals or wolves.
Seventh, they have no virtuous friends;
at the time of death, evil friends destroy their faith.
Eighth, they eat to excess.
They fell into a coma and died. Or,
while engaged in battle within the nine military arrays,
they suddenly perished.
If one were to fall ten times from a high cliff and perish,
such that their life and nature are destroyed—
just so do these ten kinds of sentient beings, at the end of their lives, cease reciting the Buddha's name and fail to attain rebirth there.
One must practice in advance so that pure karma is first accomplished;
even if one encounters difficult circumstances,
one will certainly be welcomed by Amitābha and proceed to his land.

Answer: The Pure Land is a provisional teaching for those of dull faculties. Question: Regarding the statement that the Pure Land is a provisional teaching for those of dull faculties, there was a lecturer named Sifan of the Zhongtai School during the Longxing era.
He resided for a long time at Lín píng Mountain.
His understanding was clear and his conduct was rigorous;
he reached a profound depth in the source and stream of a particular school of doctrinal and contemplative practice.
Whenever he engaged in correspondence with scholars and officials,
his answers and explanations were always brilliant and lucid in response to whatever questions were posed.
This is fully recorded in the *Huizong ji* (Anthology of the Essential Teachings). One day, Zheng Gong,
the Vice Prefect, asked:
Regarding the teachings in the sutras that clarify mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha and the aspiration to be born in the Pure Land—
is this not merely a provisional teaching for those of dull faculties?
Those of superior faculties transcend directly to the stage of Buddhahood.
"Is it not by relying on the power of another Buddha?
The Master replied,
"The predecessors of our school have rebuked this teaching, saying:"
During the Buddha’s lifetime, there were Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra;
after his parinirvāṇa, there were Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna;
in this land, there were Zhiyi and Zhiyan.
All wish to be reborn there;
are they not of dull faculties?
Śākyamuni exhorted his father, King Śuddhodana, as well as sixty thousand members of the Śākya clan to be reborn there.
Should all these be considered merely conventional vessels?
If these are taken as provisional,
what then shall serve as the ultimate reality?
In the past, Sun Shinlao also harbored doubts regarding this matter;
consequently, through discussions with Yang Cigong and Wang Minzhong,
his uncertainty was finally resolved.
Thus it is said:
"One may know that the Pure Land is not a provisional device established by the sages;
it is the true abode for fellow practitioners of Chan."
It should be known that, within our own country, there were only the two sages Yang and Wang who thoroughly understood the Pure Land.
In the preface to the *Jueyi ji* (Collection for Resolving Doubts), Yang quotes the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, saying:
Knowing that all phenomena are like reflections, with eyes and mind like water:
the Buddha does not come here,
and I do not go there.
If I wish to see Amitābha Buddha, I see him immediately according to my mind.
Know that those who focus their mindfulness will certainly behold him; this is a true word corresponding to the nature of reality.
This is not a provisional teaching.

Regarding the statement, "If one achieves the three powers through *nien-fo*, it is easy to transcend and proceed; if one achieves the three powers through *nien-fo*, it is easy to transcend and proceed to the assembly," the *Hui-zong* says:
"I have often observed people in the world..."
Previously he recited the Buddha's name;
however, when afflicted by the suffering of illness,
he became afraid even to mention the word "death."
"He merely recites the name of Avalokiteśvara to seek salvation. I said,
"This person is extremely deluded."
I shall now explain three kinds of power that can resolve your doubts and cause your mindfulness of the Buddha to become flavorful.
The first is the power of the buddha-nature inherently possessed by sentient beings.
The original mind of sentient beings inherently possesses Buddha-nature;
it is equal to that of Amitābha and not different from it.
As the Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra says:
The Buddha observes that within the minds of all sentient beings,
which are defiled by afflictions, there exists the body of a Tathāgata sitting cross-legged.
"Steadfast and unmoving,
fully endowed with the marks of virtue"—
this is precisely its meaning.
Second is the power of Amitābha’s compassionate light to gather and sustain beings.
As the sutra says:
"The Buddha-mind is great compassion."
He gathers all sentient beings with objectless compassion (*apratihata-maitrī*).
Furthermore, the Buddha possesses eighty-four thousand rays of light that gather those sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*).
That his mind does not abandon it—
this is its meaning.
Third is the power of the merit of faith and mindfulness of the Buddha.
A person who recites the Buddha’s name with faith is like a child calling out to its mother; the mother will surely protect it.
As a sutra says:
"Recall the Buddha and recite his name."
This refers to the certainty of seeing the Buddha in the present and in the future.
These three powers are like three strands of rope joined together to form a great cord, capable of pulling heavy objects to another place.
Furthermore, it is like water, fire, or a mirror: if one holds them toward the sun and draws a moxa stick near them, one will obtain fire;
likewise, if one holds them toward the moon, one will obtain water.

Now, the fact that the substance of the mirror possesses the natures of both water and fire can be used as a metaphor for the power of the Buddha-nature inherently possessed by sentient beings, which requires the light of the sun and moon to come and illuminate it.
This may be likened to the power of Amitābha’s compassionate light to gather in and protect beings.
Just as a mirror and moxa can respectively draw forth water and fire,
this may be likened to the meritorious power of reciting the Buddha’s name with faith.
These three substances must combine with water and fire for [fire] to arise;
this serves as a metaphor for how it is easy to attain birth in the Pure Land when the three powers mutually support one another.

Regarding the discernment of the mind in the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi* practice, if there is conceptualization, it is delusion. In response to the question on the Essential Principle regarding the discernment of the mind in the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi* practice: if there is conceptualization, it is delusion. The Questioner on the Essential Principle asked:
In the *Pratyutpanna Sūtra*,
one is instructed to bring Amitābha Buddha to mind in every thought-moment;
this constitutes having a mental image.
Yet later in the sutra it says:
"If the mind has conceptualization, there is delusion;
if it is without conceptualization, that is nirvana."
Why is there a contradiction between the preceding and the following?
The answer is:
that sutra first clarifies the visualization of Amitābha.
One must not be without mindfulness.
Later, when the merit of samādhi is perfected, one will see the Buddhas of the ten directions standing in the air.
At that time, one should realize that one's own mind and the Buddha-mind are identical in their true nature, which is inconceivable.
Therefore it is said:
"Where there is perception, there is delusion;
where there is no perception, that is nirvana."
This does not mean that one cannot practice visualization from the very beginning.
Furthermore, the wisdom of non-conceptuality and non-arising is perfected only upon the stage of Buddhahood;
at present, people have not yet entered the gateway of contemplative practice.
Thus, one speaks of non-arising and non-thought;
yet how could one know that what Aśvaghoṣa taught proceeds from thought to non-thought, and from speech to non-speech?
As the Mañjuśrī-prajñā Sūtra says:
It is like a person learning archery:
through long practice they become skillful,
such that later, even without conscious intent, they act with precision.
Every arrow he released hit its mark.
If a person wishes to enter the Samādhi of One Practice,
they should single-mindedly recite his name.
With thoughts succeeding one another in continuous succession,
one perceives the Buddhas of the ten directions within each thought;
thus it is known that one uses mindfulness to bring mindfulness to rest.
To dispel words with words is the orthodox path of practice for all Buddhas and patriarchs.
When Bianzhi Gong said, "Foolish people delight in going to the West," Huizong asked: [The text continues: "Bianzhi Gong, foolish people delight in going to the West. Huizong asked:
The scriptural teachings state:
"The wise ardently seek birth in the Pure Land.
Furthermore, in the *Chan Zhong* (Collection on Meditation), there is a statement by Master Zhi:
The wise know that the mind is the Buddha;
the ignorant delight in going to the Western Land.
Does this mean, then, that those who cultivate the Pure Land are ignorant?
Answer: This is likely a statement composed by later people.
Even if it were indeed the words of Master Zhi, it merely takes up the sense that "mind-only is itself Buddha."
Not to grasp at the conceptualization of Amitābha—
this is called "substituting principle for phenomena.
As the former masters said:
If principle supersedes phenomena,
then there is no distinction between purity and defilement, nor between acceptance and rejection.
If phenomena supersede principle, [the same applies].
Then there would be the distinction of abandoning suffering and attaining happiness.
One should further ask:
if phenomena and principle are as one, such that essence does not supersede appearance, [how can this be so?]
Again, how is it? He replied:
"I also know it is right there upon the autumn river."
"Where can one seek the bright moon and the reeds?
Regarding the three Bodhisattvas who vowed to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven, the *Ten Doubts Treatise* (*Shiyi lun*) states:
"Tuṣita Heaven is the abode of Maitreya."
Furthermore, there are women whom the various devas cherish and are attached to;
this is not as it is in the Pure Land of Amitābha, and so forth. Formerly, in the Western Regions, there were three bodhisattvas: Asaṅga, Vasubandhu, and Siṃhabuddhi.
We form a covenant to be born together in Tuṣita;
if one of us departs first, they shall see Maitreya and vow to return and inform the other.
Sīhabuddhi passed away previously;
he did not come for several years.
Later, Upāli passed away.
Only after three years did he arrive.
Asanga asked, "For what reason have you been so late?"
Vasubandhu said,
"I went there and listened to Maitreya’s teaching of the Dharma while seated once;
I then circumambulated him and returned immediately."
The days of those devas are long;
therefore, these three years [are calculated] according to the awakening of the lion.
Born there in the celestial palaces outside,
they become attached to the five desires;
they depart on their own and do not see Maitreya at all.
For this reason, they do not come.
Even the lesser bodhisattvas born there still cling to the five desires,
let alone ordinary worldlings.
For this reason, I exhort you to be reborn in the Western Paradise, rather than in Tuṣita.
To clarify that the purity of the mind results in the purity of the land, there is a short scroll titled *The Pure Land of the Tranquil Chamber*.
Observing his words, which were repeated with earnest sincerity,
it must have been Wang Longshu who composed this text.
Having read it, I found it quite admirable.
Regarding his critique of those who do not cultivate Pure Land practices within the Chan school, he said:
"One whose mind roams in meditative concentration and awakens to the essence of the Chan lineage is shown the Pure Land."
One must say:
"The Pure Land is mind-only;
once my own mind is pure,"
If the land is already pure,
why seek another place of rebirth?
Now, I ask this again.
Furthermore, in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra,
the Tathāgata pressed the earth with his toe and beheld the Sahā world as entirely adorned and pure.
Yet the assembly did not see it;
only the Brahma King Śikhin perceived it.
Can those who practice dhyāna today perceive a pure land as clearly as the Brahma King Śikhin did?
Moreover, since you dwell in a humble room and a dilapidated house, you will surely envy grand mansions and lofty halls;
and since you eat coarse grain with a soup of mugwort, you will surely envy rare delicacies and sweet flavors.
One who wears a tattered robe or coarse brown cloth will surely envy silk, brocade, and fine gauze;
yet if one says that the mind being pure results in the land being pure,
then such distinctions as those mentioned above are unnecessary.
How much more so when, amidst a world afflicted by the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death,
one's countenance is no different from that of those who have not yet attained awakening;
thus, one utters with the mouth words of "purity of mind" and "purity of the Pure Land."
To have one's body bound by the afflictions of this defiled land is the height of self-deception; otherwise,
one must surely trust the teachings and look up to the principles.
One should select and follow the best path from among the various approaches to the Pure Land and cultivate it.

To seek birth in the Pure Land by relying on the power of the Buddha’s vows makes it easy to be born there. Thus, Jishi said: [To seek birth in the Pure Land by relying on the power of the Buddha’s vows makes it easy to be born there].
Sentient beings who practice wholesome deeds in a general way find it difficult to achieve success because they rely solely on their own power; however,
if they practice the Pure Land method, [they will succeed].
It is established easily by relying on the power of the Buddha’s vows,
whereas it is difficult to accomplish through one's own power;
for the resolve and willpower of sentient beings are weak and inferior.
Evil karma is heavy and thick.
To oppose such heavy and thick karma with a weak and inferior mind is therefore difficult to overcome.
How much more so when one is externally thwarted by evil friends, māras, or heretics;
or when one is mired in wine, sensual beauty, wealth, and silks—
how could the wholesome dharmas one cultivates ever be easily accomplished?

That it is easy to establish [the path] by relying on the power of the Buddha's vows is truly because Amitābha’s original vow delivers those of inferior capacity, such that when the merit of even ten recitations is perfected,
one immediately goes [to the Pure Land]. This is due to the vow of this Buddha, our Protector.
Cultivating wholesome dharmas is easily established.
For example, it is like two people who wish to cross the great ocean and go to a mountain of jewels to seek treasure;
one of them plants trees.
He waited until they had grown up,
then built a boat and set out;
before long, the tree was destroyed by frost, hail, and the damage caused by humans and livestock.
There are those who ultimately fail to become accomplished;
even if they do become accomplished,
it takes a long period of time.
"How could a boat be completed so suddenly?
It is likewise difficult for one to achieve success through the cultivation of one's own power alone;
such a person does not build another boat."
While waiting there on the seashore, he happened to encounter a merchant leader traveling upon a great ship;
the man immediately went to him for refuge,
and the merchant leader took pity on him.
Even if one extends a hand to beckon them aboard the ship,
with the sails and rigging ready,
they will reach the Mountain of Jewels in the mere twinkling of an eye.
It is likewise through the power of the Buddha’s vows that one attains birth in the Western Land.
The merchant leader is like the Tathāgata who receives and guides sentient beings;
the great ship is the Great Vow of the Buddha.
Universally delivering all across the ocean is to cross over the long current of birth and death;
the Jewel Mountain is none other than the land of Ultimate Bliss.
In the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Nāgārjuna praises the Buddha as follows:
"By means of that ship of the Eightfold Path,
he is able to cross the sea that is so difficult to traverse."
This is precisely that meaning.

How magnificent! Amitābha Buddha, together with his two Bodhisattvas, boards the great vessel of the vows and sails upon the sea of birth and death, arriving here in this land of suffering and affliction, Sahā.
Summoning all sentient beings,
they board the great vessel of supreme vows and cross over the ocean of birth and death.
Reaching the western shore of nirvana,
one is surely free from the remaining aggregates (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
Regarding the phrase "attaining immortality in the Way-gate does not mean escaping the cycle of rebirth," the commentary on Master Shou’s *An-yang Fu* states:
The ten *kṣetra-rāja* jewels of the western buddha-fields,
with their long tongues, praise [the Buddha] in ways that differ from the scriptures of other paths, all saying:
A blue bird alighted and came;
it was discovered when a stone cliff collapsed.
Since there was no one capable of explaining it, [it remained unknown].
Furthermore, there is no place where they have spoken anything;
it is sufficient to know that their deceptions and fabrications cannot be relied upon,
even if they were to ascend.
Not departing from the cycle of rebirth within the three realms.
*Yebang Yigaō*, Volume Upper;
*Yebang Yigaō*, Volume Lower.
The *Shishi* (Stone-Flower) Chan monk Zongxiao of Siming compiled and annotated [this work].
Regarding the statement that one cannot be born in that land through few roots of goodness,
the *Cien Amituo Tongzan Chao* (Ci’en’s Commentary on the General Praise of Amitābha) says:
The Sūtra states:
"One cannot be born in that land through causes and conditions of even a small amount of roots of goodness or merit.
This is truly because sentient beings have previously heard the Buddha say that by means of ten recitations at the time of death, one immediately attains rebirth there.
"My life has not yet come to its end;
for now, I shall indulge in negligence.
It was in order to prevent this [thought] that [the Buddha spoke].
To say that one cannot be born in that land through even a small amount of wholesome roots,
or to say, "Today my life span is not yet exhausted," is the view of a fool.
Human life is impermanent, like a shifting candle flame.
How could it endure for long?
It is as if the Buddha were still in the world.
There were some bhikṣus practicing the contemplation of impermanence.
The Buddha asked them how they did so,
and the bhikṣus replied:
"One does not preserve the exhalation while inhaling.
The Buddha said,
"Truly, this is the attainment of the characteristic of impermanence."
The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp contains the following: One day, a student asked Chan Master Haihui, who had taught that "the mind is pure and the land is pure": [The student] asked, "..."
"I wish to be reborn in the Pure Land;
I wonder, does the Pure Land truly exist?
The Master said:
The Sūtra says:
"If you wish to attain the Pure Land,
you should purify your mind."
According to the purity of one's mind,
so too is the buddha-field pure;
if the mind is pure, [the field is pure].
Wherever one dwells, that place becomes a pure land.
It is like being born into a royal family, destined to inherit the sovereign legacy;
so too is it for one who resolves their mind toward the Buddha-way.
This leads to birth in a pure Buddha-land;
if one's mind is not pure,
then wherever one is born will be a defiled land.
Purity and defilement reside in the mind;
they do not reside in the land.

The Great Wisdom Vinaya Master demonstrated the non-duality of phenomena and principle. This Great Wisdom Vinaya Master once composed a preface for the *Jingtu ji* (Anthology on the Pure Land) by the Dharma Master Cihui of Shanyin.
The summary states:
"Throughout ancient and modern times, many who study Buddhism have been confused regarding phenomena (shì) and principle (lǐ).
They claim that as for principle, not even a speck of dust can be established."
When speaking of phenomena, the myriad forms are arrayed in profusion;
when concentrating the mind to abide in stillness, this constitutes contemplation of principle (*li-guan*);
when engaging in movement and cultivation, this constitutes practice of phenomena (*shi-xing*).
He then cited an ancient saying:
"In the ground of the ultimate reality, not a single speck of dust is admitted;
within the gateway of Buddha-works, not a single dharma is abandoned."
This is the simultaneous establishment of principle and phenomena,
and the concurrent movement of emptiness and existence.
I have once rephrased these words as follows:
In the ground of the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), there is not even a single speck of dust;
yet within the gateway of Buddha-activity (buddhakārya), not a single dharma is established.
Why is this? It is because the reality-limit inherently contains all dharmas.
How could there be even a single speck of dust missing?
Since the gateway of Buddha-works is free from all marks,
how could there be even a single dharma remaining?
In this way, one will finally perceive that principle and phenomena are as one, and existence and non-existence are non-dual.

Regarding the account of the woman who sat in meditation until death and whose bones grew into lotus flowers, the *Zasuo* (Miscellaneous Sayings) states: [The text continues with the narrative of the woman’s death and the miraculous growth of the lotuses from her remains.]
In the folk tradition of Wenzhou, there was a woman who suddenly passed away while sitting.
Later, from within her urn of ashes and bones, a single blue lotus flower sprang forth.
The multitude marveled at this.
At that time, Chan Master Zhijue Shou heard of and saw it,
and spoke a verse in praise of him, saying:
The gateway of the nature-mind is shared by the thousand sages;
the spirit returns to the Pure Land, and the lotus emerges from the ashes.
Master Yuanbian’s Discourse on the Mind-Only Pure Land: Master Yuanbian of Yanqing Monastery had a discourse titled "The Mind-Only Pure Land."
I have already transcribed the previous record.
Now, from the *Pao-chu chi* (Treasure-Bead Collection), I have further obtained its essential point, which states:
"The Pure Land of Mind-only is one and the same."
It is truly because Amitābha has realized that my own mind is his precious land,
and my own mind possesses Amitābha’s blissful realm;
though distant, it is near, never departing from a single thought-moment.
Though near, it is as distant as ten million billion lands;
it is like the bright moon in a clear blue sky reflected in the waters of many rivers—
the water does not rise up, nor does the moon descend.
The moon in the water is that which naturally reflects upon its own single horizon.
This is the "Praise of the Honored Image of Amitābha by the Dharma Master Jiekong. At the Baoyun Monastery in Siming, there was a scholar of the teachings named Sijue.
He commissioned an artisan to paint an image of Amitābha Buddha in the act of welcoming and guiding sentient beings across,
hoping thereby to increase his practice of the *nien-fo* samādhi.
He went to see Yanqing at Zhuanan.
One may observe him and bow the head, praising him with these verses:
A mass of purple-gold light, With a white jade-like radiant brow-hair;
The realm of the mind’s own nature is not high, Yet encompasses the three grades and nine ranks, And the eight virtues and four lights.
A single thought of purity immediately reveals the West.

*Praise for the Dharma-Jewel of the Ritual Text for the Liturgy of the Western Pure Land*, supplemented by the Ritual Text for the Liturgy of the Western Pure Land. At Mount Baiyun in Tiantai, there was the Dharma Master Jingyuan.
He transmitted the teachings and contemplative practices of Tiantai and once composed a liturgical text for the worship of the Western Pure Land,
which was prefaced by the Venerable Dazhi of Lingzhi and put into practice.
The composition of the text is complete;
it truly rivals the Indian original of the *Sūtra on Repentance*.
Within it, only the four sages are listed.
However, the chapter on "Praising the Dharma" was missing.
The lay practitioner Li Jie of Xiachuan devoted himself to the practice of Pure Land,
and once supplemented it, saying:
With a sincere heart, I take refuge and pay homage to the subtle, perfect vehicle and pure treasury of all Dharma-gates in the Western Land of Peace and Bliss.
The Buddha has expounded this perfect vehicle for ten kalpas; these inexhaustible Dharma-gates are as vast as space.
The wind whistles through jeweled leaves as it accords with the True Sutra, and the ripples on the golden channels explain the wondrous scriptures.
Furthermore, his transformative manifestations were heard to possess the tongue of a parrot, and his proclamations resounded with the voice of a kalaviṅka bird.
The seven scriptures exclusively praise his profound and vast meaning; the nature of phenomena is like space, beyond all verbal expression.

Chan Master Huaiyu ascended the golden terrace to be reborn in the Pure Land. According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*: Chan Master Huaiyu ascended the golden terrace to be reborn in the Pure Land. The *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song* states: [text follows].
In Taizhou there was a Chan master named Huaiyu,
who strictly observed the Vinaya rules and whose integrity was as sharp and upright as a steep cliff.
He wore only plain cloth garments and took but one meal a day;
he sat perpetually without reclining and recited the name of Amitābha Buddha fifty thousand times daily.
He regularly recited the Amitābha Sūtra three hundred thousand times.
One day, he suddenly beheld the holy assembly of the Western Paradise,
their number as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
Inside was a man carrying a silver stand who entered through a window. Yu said:
"I myself wish to attain rebirth upon the golden terrace.
Having said this, he vanished.
Thereupon, Yubei redoubled his diligent practice.
Later, he heard a voice in the sky saying,
"There is already a halo upon the Master's head."
"Please sit cross-legged and form the mudrā.
At that moment, the Buddha's light filled the room.
The Master then said, "I am leaving."
The disciple asked,
"Where are you going?
The Master spoke a verse, saying:
Pure and radiant, free from all dust and defilement;
born through transformation from a lotus flower as my parents.
I have practiced the Way for ten kalpas.
Manifesting in Jambudvīpa to weary the multitudes of suffering,
one surpasses ten kalpas through a lifetime of ascetic practice;
forever leaving the Sahā world behind, one returns to the Pure Land.
Having finished speaking, he passed away with a smile on his face.
When the Governor, Duan Huairan, saw this, he marveled at it and composed a verse in praise, saying:
My Master ascended to the First Ground in a single thought;
the music of the Buddha-land has come twice.
Only the ancient locust tree before my door remains.
The branches bend low only to hold up the Golden Terrace. Dharma Master Xianzhang vowed to attain rebirth upon the Golden Terrace.

During the Zhenghe era, there was a Dharma Master named Zhongmin, whose style name was Xianzhang. He made a vow to take the Golden Terrace as his destination for rebirth. During the Zhenghe period, there was Dharma Master Zhongmin, styled Xianzhang. He vowed to attain rebirth upon the Golden Terrace.
He was a native of Sanqu.
Having received his training at Xiangfu Temple in the prefecture,
he carried his book-basket as a youth and went to the quarters of Dharma Master Zhong in Yongjia.
After a long time, the ice became cold and the water turned deep blue;
he then went to the wheel of Master Wen at Nanping in Qiantang to complete his studies.
The assembly marveled at his arguments.
Consequently, he was called "Tiger Child.
Later, he returned to his hometown at Mount Dongfushí,
where his doorway was filled with shoes.
The Master spoke with great solemnity, saying:
"If there were not five hundred disciples beneath my seat,
